newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: PRESS DIGEST - New Zealand newspapers - Dec 24.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - New Zealand newspapers - Dec 24.

text.p: Police violence at a Waitangi Day protest in Wellington last year, which left protesters with broken bones and dislocated joints, has been condemned by a District Court judge. Judge Richard Watson, in a rider to his reserved judgment, expressed concern about the force used by police in the incident and the apparent failure to advise a demonstrator of her rights. Page 1.

Plans to introduce hidden speed cameras would almost certainly include "variables" to prevent an increase in ticketing, Police Minister Jack Elder said yesterday. Mr Elder said a proposal for police to try out hidden cameras was part of the coalition deal between NZ First and National. Page 1.

National Party treasurer Michael Cox resigned from the job yesterday, saying it would be "hypocrisy of the worst kind" to stay after the coalition deal with NZ First. However, others in National hinted that the resignation had more to do with the decision to drop his wife, Katherine O'Regan, from the ranks of ministers. Cox said that as treasurer for the past six years he had led teams that had raised millions of dollars in donations from individuals and businesses. "Many of these entities have been abused and maligned, often from behind the skirts of parliamentary privilege, by Winston Peters," Cox said. Page 2.
Families of students who died in the Cave Creek disaster last year support Conservation Minister Nick Smith's call for director-general Bill Mansfield's resignation. Page 2.

Fletcher Challenge Building said yesterday it had agreed to acquire the concrete pipe and drainage product business of Humes Industries from Adelaide Brighton Cement (NZ) for NZ$52 million. Fletcher Building shares were up five cents at $4.32 in early morning trade after the purchase was announced. They ended up three cents at $4.30. The purchase is effective from January 1, and will be funded by debt. Auckland-based Humes generated earnings before interest and tax of $7 million in the year ended June 30 from revenues of $62 million.

Manufacturers are expanding sales in the domestic market to offset the impact of the high exchange rate, the September quarter Trust Bank analysis of manufacturing shows. The analysis, prepared by Business and Economic Research for the Manufacturers Federation, shows that sales within New Zealand rose 2.4 percent in the quarter after a 1.7 percent lift in the June quarter.
Home mortgage lending rates continued to drift lower yesterday, with Hongkong Bank reducing its floating mortgage rate to 9.75 percent from 10.25 percent.

The cost of phone number portability to telecommunications companies moved into the public arena yesterday, with Telecom announcing its proposed charges for rival carriers. Until now Telecom, Bell South, Clear Communications and Telstra had discussed behind closed doors the best ways of offering customers the choice of keeping the same phone number should they wish to change carriers.

Parapine Timber was considering a couple of "suggestions" that might give the comopany a more defined future, chairman Garrick Wells said. Speaking at the company's annual meeting in Upper Hutt yesterday, Wells told a handful of shareholders that one of the suggestions was more serious than the other, but he refused to give details. Parapine made a NZ$701,000 loss for the year to August, better than the previous year's $3.7 million loss.

A police proposal to bring in hidden speed cameras needs only the blessing of the Minister of Transport, Jenny Shipley, before it can go ahead. The Minister of Police, Jack Elder, last night gave the planned trial his full support and expected it to happen if Shipley agreed. The trial is expected to involve unmarked police cars hiding along highways, rural roads and urban streets. It is understood that it will run for six months from early next year. The move contradicts police assurances made three years ago -- and present police policy -- that cameras would not be hidden.

The Britomart development in downtown Auckland will be delayed after the Auckland Regional Council decided yesterday to allow public submissions on the environmental impact of the scheme. The ARC will publicly notify three resource consent applications for the project, which may delay construction by a year and add the cost of complying with any environmental conditions imposed.

The coalition with New Zealand First has cost National its treasurer, Michael Cox. The former MP resigned yesterdy the position he has held for six years, saying that to remain would be "hypocrisy of the worst sort".

The beleaguered Director-General of Conservation, Bill Mansfield, yesterday told his staff he was determined to stay on, to bring in reforms flowing from the Cave Creek tragedy. Mansfield's future has come under question since it was reported that the new Minister of Conservation, Nick Smith, has sought his resignation.

A TeNZ-type fund based on the top 20 Australian listed stocks will be launched on the New Zealand sharemarket in February. The fund, set up by Tower Trust Services, is expected to have about $60 million in its kitty when it kicks off. That is about double the amount the stock exchange's top-10 indexed fund (TeNZ) started with when it was launched in June.
Fletcher Challenge Building has bought the New Zealand concrete pipe and drainage products businesses of Hume Industries from Australian-based Adelaide Brighton for $52 million.

Wilson and Horton shares jumped another 15 cents yesterday to $11.55 as its top-10 status attracted demand from expanding passive indexed funds. An increasing number of fund managers have set up funds, mirroring the stock exchange's TeNZ concept. As these funds grow, further shares must be bought to maintain their respective indexed weighting.
